items.word: must + infinitive (present deduction) | That must be an electric car – it isn't making any noise at all.
items.source_reason: Deduction about something true in the present.
items.provided_sentence: That must be an electric car – it isn't making any noise at all.

grammar_card.sentence: That must be an electric car – it isn't making any noise at all.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to express a strong logical conclusion about the present based on available evidence.
breakdown: 'must' + base verb (infinitive without 'to')
Shows certainty about a present situation or fact
Based on deduction or logical reasoning
Example refers to current reality, not past or future
grammar_card.usage: Use 'must + infinitive' to say what you believe is true now after thinking about the facts or evidence.
grammar_card.context_example: That must be an electric car – it isn't making any noise at all.
contrasts: 'must' (deduction) vs 'might/may/could' (possibility or less certain deduction)
'must' + infinitive (present deduction) vs 'must have' + past participle (past deduction)
'must' for present deduction vs 'should' for advice or expectation
common_mistakes: Using 'must to' instead of 'must' + infinitive: Incorrect - 'That must to be true.' Correct - 'That must be true.'
Confusing 'must' (deduction) with obligation: Incorrect - 'You must be home now' (meaning deduction). Correct for obligation - 'You must come home now.'

items.word: must have + past participle (past deduction) | You must have seen him – he was standing right in front of you!
items.source_reason: Deduction about something true or happened in the past.
items.provided_sentence: You must have seen him – he was standing right in front of you!

grammar_card.sentence: You must have seen him – he was standing right in front of you!
grammar_card.meaning: This structure expresses a strong conclusion or guess about something that happened in the past, based on evidence or reasoning.
breakdown: must have = expresses certainty or strong belief about the past
past participle = the verb form used after must have (e.g., seen, done, gone)
used to make deductions about past events
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you are almost sure or deducing something that happened in the past.
grammar_card.context_example: You must have seen him – he was standing right in front of you!
contrasts: might have + past participle: weaker possibility about the past
could have + past participle: suggesting ability or possibility in the past
should have + past participle: expressing past advice or expectation
common_mistakes: You must saw him -> You must have seen him
You must have saw him -> You must have seen him

items.word: can't + continuous infinitive (present ongoing impossibility) | They can't be playing very well – they're losing 3–0.
items.source_reason: Deduction about an action that is almost certainly not true/happening in the present.
items.provided_sentence: They can't be playing very well – they're losing 3–0.

grammar_card.sentence: They can't be playing very well – they're losing 3–0.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to express that something is almost certainly not happening right now or is impossible in the present moment.
breakdown: 'Can't' expresses impossibility or strong doubt.
The continuous infinitive (be + verb-ing) shows an action ongoing in the present.
Together, they express that the action is unlikely or impossible right now.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to say you believe something is not true or not happening at the moment, based on evidence or logic.
grammar_card.context_example: They can't be playing very well – they're losing 3–0.
contrasts: Can't + base verb – expresses general inability (e.g., 'They can't play well.').
Must + continuous infinitive – expresses strong belief that something is happening (e.g., 'They must be playing well.').
'Can't + continuous infinitive' negates ongoing actions, while 'can't + base verb' negates abilities or possibilities generally.
common_mistakes: Using 'can't' with base verb instead of continuous infinitive: 'They can't play very well' (lacks present ongoing meaning).
Using 'can't be playing' to express future impossibility, e.g., 'They can't be playing tomorrow' (should use 'will not be playing').

items.word: can't / couldn't have + past participle (past impossibility) | You can't / couldn't have spent very long on this essay – you've only written 100 words.
items.source_reason: Deduction about something that was almost certainly not true/didn't happen in the past.
items.grammar_target: can't / couldn't have + past participle (past impossibility)
items.provided_sentence: You can't / couldn't have spent very long on this essay – you've only written 100 words.

grammar_card.sentence: You can't / couldn't have spent very long on this essay – you've only written 100 words.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to say that something definitely did not happen or was not possible in the past.
grammar_card.structure: can't / couldn't have + past participle (past impossibility)
breakdown: Can't / couldn't have shows past impossibility or strong disbelief about a past action.
The past participle forms the perfect part, referring to a completed past action.
Used to express certainty that something didn't happen.
grammar_card.usage: We use 'can't/couldn't have + past participle' when we are almost sure something wasn’t true or didn’t happen in the past.
grammar_card.context_example: You can't / couldn't have spent very long on this essay – you've only written 100 words.
contrasts: Must have + past participle: shows strong certainty that something did happen.
May have / might have + past participle: expresses possibility about a past action.
Could have + past participle: talks about past ability or possibility, sometimes regret.
common_mistakes: Using base verb instead of past participle: 'You can't have spend' → corrected: 'You can't have spent'.
Confusing can't with may: 'You may have spent very long' (possible) vs. 'You can't have spent very long' (not possible).

items.word: may / might / could + infinitive (present possibility) | He may / might / could be off sick.
items.source_reason: Expressing possibility in the present.
items.provided_sentence: He may / might / could be off sick.

grammar_card.sentence: He may / might / could be off sick.
grammar_card.meaning: These modal verbs show that there is a possibility something is true or happening now.
breakdown: Use 'may', 'might', or 'could' before the base form of a verb to talk about something possible now.
'He may be off sick' means it is possible he is sick today.
'Might' often suggests a slightly smaller chance than 'may'.
'Could' can also show possibility, often with a similar meaning.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to express that you think something is possibly true in the present but you are not sure.
grammar_card.context_example: He may / might / could be off sick.
contrasts: 'May/might/could be' vs. 'will be': 'may be' shows possibility; 'will be' shows certainty.
'May/might/could be' vs. 'is': 'is' states fact; 'may be' shows uncertain possibility.
'Might' vs. 'may': 'might' is sometimes used for less certain possibilities.
common_mistakes: Incorrect: He may/might/could is off sick. Correct: He may/might/could be off sick.
Incorrect: He may/might/could off sick. Correct: He may/might/could be off sick.

items.word: may / might / could have + past participle (past possibility) | Do you think someone may / might / could have taken them?
items.source_reason: Expressing possibility in the past.
items.grammar_target: may / might / could have + past participle (past possibility)
items.provided_sentence: Do you think someone may / might / could have taken them?

grammar_card.sentence: Do you think someone may / might / could have taken them?
grammar_card.meaning: Expressing possibility about something that happened in the past.
grammar_card.structure: may / might / could have + past participle (past possibility)
breakdown: may / might / could express possibility or uncertainty
have + past participle refers to an action in the past
used to speculate about past events that are not confirmed
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you want to say that something was possibly true or happened in the past, but you are not certain.
grammar_card.context_example: Do you think someone may / might / could have taken them?
contrasts: must have + past participle: expresses a strong certainty about a past event
can't have + past participle: expresses impossibility about a past event
will have + past participle: expresses a logical conclusion about a past event
common_mistakes: Incorrect: He might has gone home. Correct: He might have gone home.
Incorrect: She could took the keys. Correct: She could have taken the keys.

items.word: may / might not have + past participle (past negative possibility) | He may / might not have heard the message I left.
items.source_reason: Expressing negative possibility in the past.
items.grammar_target: may / might not have + past participle (past negative possibility)
items.provided_sentence: He may / might not have heard the message I left.

grammar_card.sentence: He may / might not have heard the message I left.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to express that it is possible someone did not do or experience something in the past.
grammar_card.structure: may / might not have + past participle (past negative possibility)
breakdown: may / might not = expresses possibility that something did NOT happen
have + past participle = refers to a past action or event
This structure indicates uncertainty about a past negative event
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you want to say something probably didn’t happen, but you are not completely sure.
grammar_card.context_example: He may / might not have heard the message I left.
contrasts: may / might have + past participle = expresses positive possibility in the past (e.g., He may have heard the message).
did not + base verb = definite negative statement about the past (e.g., He did not hear the message).
could not have + past participle = expresses certainty that something did NOT happen in the past (e.g., He could not have heard the message).
common_mistakes: He might not have hear the message. → correct: heard
He may not have hears the message. → correct: heard

items.word: should / ought to + infinitive (expected present/future situation) | If I post the letter today, it should / ought to arrive on Friday.
items.source_reason: Describing a situation we expect to happen.
items.grammar_target: should / ought to + infinitive (expected present/future situation)
items.provided_sentence: If I post the letter today, it should / ought to arrive on Friday.

grammar_card.sentence: If I post the letter today, it should / ought to arrive on Friday.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to talk about an expected or probable present or future situation based on a condition.
grammar_card.structure: should / ought to + infinitive (expected present/future situation)
breakdown: Use 'should' or 'ought to' + base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to')
'Should' and 'ought to' express expectation or probability
Often used with 'if' to talk about conditions and likely results
Refers to something likely true now or in the future
grammar_card.usage: To express what is expected or likely to happen as a result of a present or future condition.
grammar_card.context_example: If I post the letter today, it should / ought to arrive on Friday.
contrasts: 'will' + infinitive: states a definite future action (e.g., 'It will arrive on Friday.')
'must' + infinitive: expresses strong certainty or necessity (e.g., 'It must arrive on Friday.')
Present simple for facts rather than expected outcomes (e.g., 'If I post the letter today, it arrives on Friday.')
common_mistakes: Using 'should to' instead of 'should' + infinitive: Incorrect: 'should to arrive', Correct: 'should arrive'
Confusing 'ought to' with 'ought': 'ought' needs 'to' plus infinitive in this structure
Using past tense after 'should'/'ought to' in future expectation: Incorrect: 'If I post, it should arrived', Correct: 'should arrive'

items.word: should / ought to have + past participle (expected past situation) | I posted the letter a week ago, it should / ought to have arrived by now.
items.source_reason: Describing a situation we would expect to have happened in the past.
items.grammar_target: should / ought to have + past participle (expected past situation)
items.provided_sentence: I posted the letter a week ago, it should / ought to have arrived by now.

grammar_card.sentence: I posted the letter a week ago, it should / ought to have arrived by now.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to express an expectation that something was completed or happened in the past.
grammar_card.structure: should / ought to have + past participle (expected past situation)
breakdown: 'should / ought to have' = expressing expectation or probability about a past action
'Past participle' = describes the completed action
Used for situations we expect to have happened by now, but are unsure
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you believe something was probably done or happened already, but you are not certain.
grammar_card.context_example: I posted the letter a week ago, it should / ought to have arrived by now.
contrasts: 'should have + past participle' vs. 'should + base verb' (present/future advice)
'ought to have + past participle' vs. 'must have + past participle' (expectation vs. certainty)
'should / ought to have' vs. 'could have' (expectation vs. possibility)
common_mistakes: I should arrived by now. → I should have arrived by now.
He ought to have went there. → He ought to have gone there.

items.word: mustn't / mustn't have (not for speculation) | You mustn't be late for the meeting.
items.source_rule: We don't use *mustn't / mustn't have* with this meaning [speculation/deduction].
items.source_reason: The rule explicitly states not to use *mustn't / mustn't have* for speculation. This is an example of correct usage for prohibition.
items.provided_sentence: You mustn't be late for the meeting.

grammar_card.sentence: You mustn't be late for the meeting.
grammar_card.meaning: This shows a strong prohibition. It means 'It is not allowed to be late.'
breakdown: 'mustn't' = prohibition (not allowed)
Used to tell someone what they must not do
'mustn't have' is not used for guessing/speculation
Focus is on rules or strong advice
grammar_card.usage:
Use 'mustn't' to express that something is forbidden or not allowed. Do NOT use 'mustn't' or 'mustn't have' to guess about the past or make speculations.

Source note: We don't use *mustn't / mustn't have* with this meaning [speculation/deduction].
grammar_card.context_example: You mustn't be late for the meeting.
contrasts: 'must' = obligation or strong advice (You must finish it)
'can't' = express impossibility or denial (He can't be here now)
'must have' = present conclusion about the past (She must have left already)
common_mistakes: Incorrect: You mustn't have been late yesterday. Correct: You couldn't have been late yesterday.
Incorrect: He mustn't be at home (to guess). Correct: He can't be at home.
Incorrect: You mustn't go to the party (when giving permission). Correct: You don't have to go to the party.

items.word: must + infinitive (deduction about habitual action) | He must work really hard.
items.source_reason: Deduction about a habitual action.
items.provided_sentence: He must work really hard.

grammar_card.sentence: He must work really hard.
grammar_card.meaning: We use 'must + infinitive' to make a strong guess or deduction about someone's regular or habitual action based on evidence or reasoning.
breakdown: 'must' expresses a logical conclusion
followed by the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to')
used here to guess what a person usually does (habit)
example: 'He must work really hard' means we believe he works hard every day
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you want to say that you are almost sure about someone's habitual actions from what you observe or know.
grammar_card.context_example: He must work really hard.
contrasts: 'must + infinitive' shows deduction, while 'can + infinitive' shows ability or permission
'must + infinitive' (deduction) vs 'must be + verb-ing' (deduction about something happening now)
'must + infinitive' talks about habitual actions deduced; 'must have + past participle' talks about past actions deduced
common_mistakes: He must working really hard. → He must work really hard.
He must to work really hard. → He must work really hard.

items.word: must + continuous infinitive (deduction about action in progress) | He must still be working.
items.source_reason: Deduction about an action in progress at the moment of speaking.
items.grammar_target: must + continuous infinitive (deduction about action in progress)
items.provided_sentence: He must still be working.

grammar_card.sentence: He must still be working.
grammar_card.meaning: Used to express a strong deduction that an action is happening right now.
grammar_card.structure: must + continuous infinitive (deduction about action in progress)
breakdown: 'must' expresses certainty or strong belief
continuous infinitive (be + verb+ing) shows the action is in progress
'still' indicates the action continues at the moment
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you are almost sure something is happening at this moment, based on evidence or reasoning.
grammar_card.context_example: He must still be working.
contrasts: must + base verb (deduction about general truth): He must work hard.
might + continuous infinitive (possibility of ongoing action): He might still be working.
must have + past participle (deduction about past action): He must have finished.
common_mistakes: He must still working. -> He must still be working.
He must be work. -> He must be working.

items.word: be bound / sure to + infinitive | He's bound / sure to be here in a minute.
items.source_reason: Saying that something is certain to be true or to happen.
items.provided_sentence: He's bound / sure to be here in a minute.

grammar_card.sentence: He's bound / sure to be here in a minute.
grammar_card.meaning: This expression means something is certain or very likely to happen.
breakdown: 'Be bound to' or 'be sure to' + base verb (infinitive without 'to')
Used to express strong certainty about a future event
In the sentence, 'He's' is the contraction of 'He is', followed by 'bound / sure to' + verb
grammar_card.usage: Use 'be bound to' or 'be sure to' to say that something will definitely or very likely happen.
grammar_card.context_example: He's bound / sure to be here in a minute.
contrasts: 'Will' expresses future but doesn't always imply certainty (e.g., He will come, but it might not be sure)
Using 'might be' or 'may be' shows possibility, not certainty
'Be bound to' is stronger than 'going to' in expressing inevitability
common_mistakes: He's bound to be here in a minute. (correct) vs. He's bound to being here in a minute. (incorrect)
She sure to know the answer. (incorrect) → She is sure to know the answer. (correct)

items.word: subject + be likely / unlikely to + infinitive | I think she's likely / unlikely to agree to our proposal.
items.source_reason: Using 'likely / unlikely' as adjectives with a subject.
items.grammar_target: subject + be likely / unlikely to + infinitive
items.provided_sentence: I think she's likely / unlikely to agree to our proposal.

grammar_card.sentence: I think she's likely / unlikely to agree to our proposal.
grammar_card.meaning: It expresses the probability that the subject (she) will or will not do something (agree to our proposal).
grammar_card.structure: subject + be likely / unlikely to + infinitive
breakdown: 'subject' is the person or thing doing the action.
'be likely / unlikely to' describes probability or chance.
Follow with the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to') after 'to'.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to talk about how probable it is that someone will do a specific action.
grammar_card.context_example: I think she's likely / unlikely to agree to our proposal.
contrasts: 'might / may + base verb' for possibility without certainty.
'will + base verb' for definite future actions.
'probably + verb' as an adverb expressing likelihood.
common_mistakes: Using 'likely' without 'to' + infinitive (Incorrect: She's likely agree. Correct: She's likely to agree.)
Using the wrong verb form after 'to' (Incorrect: She's likely to agreeing. Correct: She's likely to agree.)

items.word: It is likely / unlikely that + clause | It is likely / unlikely that the government will raise interest rates this year.
items.source_reason: Using 'likely / unlikely' as adjectives with 'it is...that'.
items.grammar_target: It is likely / unlikely that + clause
items.provided_sentence: It is likely / unlikely that the government will raise interest rates this year.

grammar_card.sentence: It is likely / unlikely that the government will raise interest rates this year.
grammar_card.meaning: This structure is used to express the probability or expectation that something will or will not happen.
grammar_card.structure: It is likely / unlikely that + clause
breakdown: ‘It is likely’ means there is a good chance something will happen.
‘It is unlikely’ means there is a low chance something will happen.
This is followed by a clause (a subject + verb).
Example: The government will raise interest rates this year.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure when you want to talk about how probable it is that a certain event or action will take place.
grammar_card.context_example: It is likely / unlikely that the government will raise interest rates this year.
contrasts: ‘It is possible that’ focuses on possibility without suggesting likelihood.
‘It might be that’ is less certain than ‘It is likely that’.
‘Probably’ + clause is a simpler way to express likelihood.
common_mistakes: Incorrect: It is likely that will the government raise rates this year. (Correct: It is likely that the government will raise rates this year.)
Incorrect: It is unlikely the government raise interest rates this year. (Correct: It is unlikely that the government will raise interest rates this year.)

items.word: adverb position: auxiliary + definitely + main verb | She'll definitely pass the exam.
items.source_reason: Position of 'definitely' when there is an auxiliary verb.
items.grammar_target: adverb position: auxiliary + definitely + main verb
items.provided_sentence: She'll definitely pass the exam.

grammar_card.sentence: She'll definitely pass the exam.
grammar_card.meaning: 'Definitely' is used here to show certainty or strong confidence about the action. It is placed after the auxiliary verb and before the main verb.
grammar_card.structure: adverb position: auxiliary + definitely + main verb
breakdown: 'She'll' is the contraction of 'She will' (auxiliary verb + subject).
'Definitely' is the adverb that shows certainty.
'Pass' is the main verb following 'definitely'.
The adverb 'definitely' comes between the auxiliary and the main verb.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to express strong certainty about a future action with auxiliary verbs like 'will', 'can', or 'should'.
grammar_card.context_example: She'll definitely pass the exam.
contrasts: 'Definitely' after the main verb: She'll pass definitely the exam. (Incorrect placement)
When no auxiliary verb is present, 'definitely' goes before the main verb: She definitely passes the exam.
'Definitely' before the auxiliary verb is less common: Definitely she'll pass the exam.
common_mistakes: She'll pass definitely the exam. → She'll definitely pass the exam.
She definitely will pass the exam. (possible but less common)
She will passes definitely the exam. → She'll definitely pass the exam.

items.word: adverb position: definitely + negative auxiliary | She definitely won't pass the exam.
items.source_reason: Position of 'definitely' in a negative sentence with an auxiliary verb.
items.provided_sentence: She definitely won't pass the exam.

grammar_card.sentence: She definitely won't pass the exam.
grammar_card.meaning: The adverb 'definitely' is used here to emphasize a strong certainty about a negative statement made with the auxiliary verb 'won't' (will not).
breakdown: 'definitely' is placed before the negative auxiliary verb 'won't'.
'won't' is a contraction of 'will not', used to make negative future statements.
The adverb adds emphasis to the certainty of the negative outcome.
grammar_card.usage: Use 'definitely' before negative auxiliaries (won't, can't, don't, etc.) to stress firm certainty in a negative sentence.
grammar_card.context_example: She definitely won't pass the exam.
contrasts: Position of 'definitely' before negative auxiliaries, not after: 'She won't definitely pass' (incorrect).
Using 'definitely' in positive sentences: 'She will definitely pass the exam.' (positive certainty).
Placing 'definitely' after the main verb: 'She won't pass definitely the exam' (incorrect).
common_mistakes: 'She won't definitely pass the exam.' → Correct: 'She definitely won't pass the exam.'
'She definitely passes not the exam.' → Correct: 'She definitely won't pass the exam.'

items.word: adverb position: auxiliary + probably + be | He'll probably be here around 8.00.
items.source_reason: Position of 'probably' with 'be' when there is an auxiliary verb.
items.provided_sentence: He'll probably be here around 8.00.

grammar_card.sentence: He'll probably be here around 8.00.
grammar_card.meaning: Shows where the adverb 'probably' is placed between the auxiliary verb and the main verb 'be' to express likelihood.
breakdown: 'He'll' = 'He will' (auxiliary verb 'will')
'probably' comes after the auxiliary verb
'be' is the main verb following 'probably'
The sentence means he is likely to arrive around 8.00
grammar_card.usage: 'Probably' is often placed between an auxiliary and the main verb to show that something is likely but not certain.
grammar_card.context_example: He'll probably be here around 8.00.
contrasts: 'Probably' before the auxiliary: Probably he'll be here around 8.00. (less common, sounds formal or awkward)
'Probably' after the main verb: He'll be probably here around 8.00. (incorrect word order)
Without auxiliary: He probably is here around 8.00. (informal, less common in future tense)
common_mistakes: He'll be probably here around 8.00. → Correct: He'll probably be here around 8.00.
Probably he'll be here around 8.00. (awkward) → Correct: He'll probably be here around 8.00.

items.word: adverb position: probably + negative auxiliary + be | He probably won't be here until about 8.15.
items.source_reason: Position of 'probably' with 'be' in a negative sentence with an auxiliary verb.
items.grammar_target: adverb position: probably + negative auxiliary + be
items.provided_sentence: He probably won't be here until about 8.15.

grammar_card.sentence: He probably won't be here until about 8.15.
grammar_card.meaning: This structure shows where the adverb 'probably' is placed before the negative auxiliary verb 'won't' and the verb 'be' to express a likely negative event.
grammar_card.structure: adverb position: probably + negative auxiliary + be
breakdown: 'Probably' is an adverb expressing likelihood.
The negative auxiliary 'won't' (will not) comes after 'probably'.
The main verb 'be' follows the auxiliary verb.
The order is: probably + won't + be.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to say something is unlikely or expected not to happen, with a focus on possibility.
grammar_card.context_example: He probably won't be here until about 8.15.
contrasts: 'Probably' before positive auxiliary: She probably is coming later.
Adverb after negative auxiliary: He won't probably be here (less common/wrong).
Different adverb position with modal verbs: She might not be ready.
common_mistakes: He won't probably be here until about 8.15. → Correct: He probably won't be here until about 8.15.
He probably not will be here until about 8.15. → Correct: He probably won't be here until about 8.15.

items.word: adverb position: 'be' verb + adverb (affirmative) | He's probably British.
items.source_reason: Position of adverbs of speculation after the 'be' verb in affirmative sentences.
items.provided_sentence: He's probably British.

grammar_card.sentence: He's probably British.
grammar_card.meaning: This structure shows the position of adverbs of speculation after the 'be' verb in affirmative sentences.
breakdown: 'He' is the subject.
'is' is the 'be' verb.
'probably' is the adverb of speculation placed after 'be'.
'British' is the adjective complement.
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to place adverbs directly after the 'be' verb to express certainty, probability, or possibility about the subject in affirmative sentences.
grammar_card.context_example: He's probably British.
contrasts: Adverbs of frequency usually come before the main verb but after 'be' verb here: She is always happy.
In negative sentences with 'be', adverb placement changes: He isn't probably British (incorrect) vs. He probably isn't British (correct).
Adverbs can be placed differently with other verbs: He probably lives in London.
common_mistakes: He's British probably. (Incorrect – adverb should be after 'be')
He's maybe British. (Less natural; use 'probably' instead)
He's probably is British. (Incorrect word order)

items.word: adverb position: adverb + 'be' verb (negative) | The painting definitely isn't genuine.
items.source_reason: Position of adverbs of speculation before the 'be' verb in negative sentences.
items.provided_sentence: The painting definitely isn't genuine.

grammar_card.sentence: The painting definitely isn't genuine.
grammar_card.meaning: This structure shows that adverbs like 'definitely' can be placed immediately before the negative 'be' verb to emphasize certainty or emphasis in a negative sentence.
breakdown: 'definitely' is the adverb of certainty
'isn't' is the negative form of the 'be' verb
The adverb comes directly before the negative 'be' verb
This placement adds emphasis to the negation
grammar_card.usage: Use this structure to clearly express a strong opinion or certainty when negating with forms of 'be' (isn't, aren't, wasn't, weren't). It highlights the adverb's role in modifying the verb.
grammar_card.context_example: The painting definitely isn't genuine.
contrasts: Adverb after the negative be verb: 'The painting isn't definitely genuine.' (less natural, less emphasis)
Adverb before affirmative be verb: 'The painting is definitely genuine.'
Adverb at the start of the sentence: 'Definitely, the painting isn't genuine.' (more formal or emphatic)
common_mistakes: 'The painting isn't definitely genuine.' → Adverb should come before the negative be verb.
'The painting definitely not is genuine.' → Incorrect word order; adverb must be before negative verb.
'The painting isn't genuine definitely.' → Adverb misplaced after adjective, which sounds unnatural here.
